title: My Parents Paid A One Hundred Eighty Thousand Dollar Entrance Fee To Move Into A Fancy Arizona Retirement Community After A Salesman Promised It Was Ninety Percent Refundable, But My Father Died Three Weeks Later And They Told My Mother Her
excerpt: My parents spent forty-six winters in Minnesota. My father, Harold, was a high school math teacher in a small town near Duluth. My mother, Marlene, was a nurse at the regional hospital. blocks.text: PART 1 — THE DESERT

My parents spent forty-six winters in Minnesota. My father, Harold, was a high school math teacher in a small town near Duluth. My mother, Marlene, was a nurse at the regional hospital. They raised three kids in a drafty farmhouse with a woodstove, and every January, when the temperature dropped to thirty below, Dad would say, “Someday, Marlene. Someday we’re going to Arizona.”

They were seventy-nine and seventy-seven. They sold the farmhouse. After paying off what was left of the mortgage and moving costs, they had about two hundred thousand dollars. That, plus their pensions and Social Security, was everything they had.

They’d toured several retirement communities in Arizona on a trip the winter before. They fell in love with one outside Scottsdale. It was what’s called a continuing care retirement community, or CCRC. Independent living apartments, with assisted living and a nursing center on the same campus, so residents can stay in one place as their needs change.
It had a pool, a golf course, a library, a chapel, and a dining room with white tablecloths. The apartment they chose had a little patio facing the mountains.
To move in, they had to pay an “entrance fee.” One hundred eighty thousand dollars. Plus a monthly fee for services.

That’s how most CCRCs work. The entrance fee helps guarantee residents access to care for life. Some entrance fees are partly refundable, if a resident leaves or dies. Some aren’t. The refundable plans usually cost more upfront.
Dad asked the salesman about the refund. The salesman’s answer was the reason they chose this community over the others.
“Ninety percent refundable,” he said. “If anything ever happens, the money goes back to your family.”
Someday, Marlene. Someday we’re going to Arizona.
PART 2 — THREE WEEKS
My parents moved into their new apartment on October first.

They were so happy. Mom sent me photos every day. The sunset over the mountains. The pool. Dad in a short-sleeved shirt in October, grinning like a kid. “No snow shovel,” he texted. “I’m never going back.”
They joined a water aerobics class. Dad found a group of retired men who played cribbage every afternoon. Mom signed up to volunteer at the community’s library.
Three weeks after they moved in, on a Tuesday morning, Dad had a stroke.
Mom found him on the bathroom floor. The community’s emergency team responded within minutes. An ambulance took him to the hospital in Scottsdale.
I flew in from Denver that afternoon. My brother flew in from Minneapolis, and my sister from Seattle.
Dad never woke up. He died four days later, with all of us around his bed.
He was seventy-nine. He’d waited forty-six winters for Arizona, and he got three weeks.

After the funeral, Mom went back to the apartment. She tried. She really did. But everything reminded her of him. The patio where they’d watched the sunset. The cribbage board on the coffee table. His golf shoes by the door, still with the price tag on them.
She couldn’t sleep there. She couldn’t eat in the dining room, where everyone knew they’d been a couple. She didn’t know anyone in Arizona except the people she’d met in three weeks.
Six weeks after Dad died, she called me.
“Sarah,” she said, “I want to come home. Not to Minnesota. To you. I want to live near you in Denver.”
He’d waited forty-six winters for Arizona, and he got three weeks.
PART 3 — ZERO

I’m the oldest. My name is Sarah. I live in Denver with my husband and two teenagers. I told Mom she could live near us. There’s a nice independent living apartment complex ten minutes from our house. We’d help her move.

But first, she needed her entrance fee back. One hundred eighty thousand dollars. Ninety percent refundable, the salesman had said. A hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars. That was what she’d live on for the rest of her life.
Mom went to the community’s administration office and told them she’d decided to move out. She asked about the refund.
The administrator was polite. She expressed her condolences. She pulled up Mom’s file.
Then she said Mom and Dad had signed a non-refundable contract.
Mom thought she’d misheard. She said the salesman had told them it was ninety percent refundable. She said that was why they’d chosen this community.

The administrator said that the community offered several plans. The ninety-percent refundable plan was a different plan, with a higher entrance fee, two hundred ninety thousand dollars. She said my parents had signed the “Traditional” plan, which was non-refundable after a short trial period.
She said Mom was welcome to stay, of course. She’d paid for lifetime care. But if she left, the money stayed with the community.
Mom called me from her car in the parking lot. She was crying so hard I could barely understand her.
“A hundred and eighty thousand dollars, Sarah. Everything from the farm. Your father worked thirty-eight years for that.”
After I talked to Mom that night, I called my brother and sister. We set up a video call.
My brother, Tom, is a farmer near Duluth, like Dad’s father was. He’s quiet and practical. My sister, Beth, is a high school English teacher in Seattle. She’s the emotional one.
Beth cried. Tom didn’t say anything for a long time. Then he said, “Dad asked about the refund. I was there. I heard him.”

It turned out Tom had gone on the second tour with Mom and Dad, the summer before. He’d been standing in the model apartment when Dad asked the salesman. He remembered it clearly, because Dad had made the salesman repeat himself.
“Dad said, ‘Ninety percent, even if we die the first year?’ And the guy laughed and said, ‘Even if you die the first week, Harold. That money goes to your kids.'”
Nobody on the call said anything after that.
If she left, the money stayed with the community.
PART 4 — THE CPA

I’m a CPA. A certified public accountant. I’ve worked for twenty-two years, mostly auditing businesses and nonprofit organizations, including a few health care organizations. I read contracts and financial statements for a living.
So I did what I’d do for any client. I asked for the documents.

Mom requested copies of everything from the community: the residence agreement, any addendums, the sales materials, and anything she and Dad had signed. By law in Arizona, and in many states, CCRCs have to provide prospective residents with a detailed disclosure statement and contract.

The community sent the residence agreement. It was forty-seven pages. It said, on page three, under “Entrance Fee Plan”: “Traditional Plan.” And on page nine, under “Refunds”: “The Traditional Plan Entrance Fee is non-refundable after the expiration of the 90-day rescission period, except as required by law.”
Dad and Mom had signed and initialed every page.
Mom was devastated. “I don’t understand,” she said. “He told us ninety percent. Your father asked him twice.”
I believed her. But I also knew that a signed contract is a signed contract. If the contract said non-refundable, it was going to be very hard to argue.
“Did you and Dad keep anything else from the sales process? Brochures? Notes? Emails?”
Mom thought about it. “Your father kept everything in a folder. He labeled it ‘Arizona.’ It’s in one of the boxes in the storage closet.”
My dad was a math teacher. He kept records of everything.
I flew to Arizona that weekend and opened the box.
He told us ninety percent. Your father asked him twice.
PART 5 — THE FOLDER
The folder was labeled in Dad’s neat block letters: “ARIZONA – CCRC.”

Inside were brochures from four different communities, with Dad’s notes in the margins. Comparison charts he’d made on graph paper, of course. Monthly fees. Distances to hospitals. Golf course ratings.
